name: Division No. 1

storage_detail.nearest_well: Core Energy Otsego County EOR Operations

rationale: Diffuse wet animal manure / biosolids, low nutrient status, poor geologic storage access (no affordable route to a storage well) -> wet feedstock far from affordable geologic storage favors hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) to a stable bio-crude (~30% CDR efficiency): it handles the wet biomass without drying and densifies the carbon for haulage to a distant well. Pricier than direct injection, so used only where storage is distant.
caveats: Transport to the nearest well exceeds $100/tCO₂ for this pathway's payload — defaulted to a storage-independent option or densified bio-oil.

ranked.label: Bio-oil (hydrothermal liquefaction)
pros: Handles WET biomass (manure/biosolids) directly — no drying needed
Hydrothermal liquefaction densifies the carbon into a stable bio-crude, cheap to haul to distant wells
Viable where wet-slurry injection/AD would need nearby geologic storage
Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Net of counterfactual debits: 50% gross − 9 pts soil carbon the spread manure would have built (50-yr) − 11 pts replacement fertilizer
Transport to the nearest operating well ~$115/tCO₂ — exceeds the $100/tCO₂ viability cap, so this pathway is not viable here
Higher cost and earlier-stage than pyrolysis or direct injection
Lower CDR efficiency than slurry injection (~50% vs >90%)

ranked.label: Biomass waste injection
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)
Cheaper on balance than bio-oil where wells are near
PFAS destruction; disposes problematic wet wastes
cons: Net of counterfactual debits: 90% gross − 9 pts soil carbon the spread manure would have built (50-yr) − 11 pts replacement fertilizer
Transport to the nearest operating well ~$663/tCO₂ — exceeds the $100/tCO₂ viability cap, so this pathway is not viable here
No emissions-avoiding co-product
Hauling bulky, less-carbon-dense biomass is costly if wells are far

rationale: No strong near-term BiCRS pathway here: municipal waste is the only significant feedstock but there is no waste-to-energy plant within range to retrofit with capture (and MSW is landfilled, not a removal feedstock), while other biomass — agricultural and forestry residues, manure — is limited. The options below are marginal at best.

ranked.label: Biomass burial
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)
Simple and low-cost; needs no geologic CO2 storage
Works for distributed biomass
Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Durability still being validated (Frontier prepurchase, not offtake)
No emissions-avoiding co-product; nutrient-export risk with ag residues

ranked.label: Biochar
pros: Returns nutrients to soils, improving yields
Distributed and storage-independent; simple and near-term
Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Low CDR efficiency (~30%)
Durability and verification questions; Frontier's lower-preference pathway

name: Hamilton

storage_detail.nearest_well: Core Energy Otsego County EOR Operations

cons: Lower CDR efficiency than direct injection (~65% vs >90%)
Needs dry/solid biomass — not for wet feedstocks
Higher $/t than injection where storage is proximate

Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Low CDR efficiency (~30%)
Durability and verification questions; Frontier's lower-preference pathway

cons: Durability still being validated (Frontier prepurchase, not offtake)

name: Niagara

storage_detail.nearest_well: Core Energy Otsego County EOR Operations

rationale: Diffuse wet animal manure / biosolids, moderate nutrient status, moderate geologic storage access (~$92/tCO₂ delivered over ~1953 km to Archer Daniels Midland Co.) -> much of the manure here already flows to anaerobic digesters, so AD+CCS retrofits existing biogas plants by capturing the near-pure CO2 its biomethane upgrading already vents (18% of the manure carbon; the RNG carbon is avoidance, not CDR), and is preferred over injection.
caveats: Transport to the nearest well exceeds $100/tCO₂ for this pathway's payload — defaulted to a storage-independent option or densified bio-oil.

ranked.label: AD RNG + CCS (upgrading CO₂)
pros: Manure is already digested here — AD+CCS retrofits existing biogas plants
Captures the near-pure CO2 already vented by biogas upgrading — cheap capture
RNG co-product displaces fossil gas; retrofits an existing biomethane plant
Digestate returns nutrients to fields
cons: Low CDR efficiency (~18% of manure carbon): the RNG carbon is combusted downstream (avoidance, not CDR)
Methane slip from digestion/upgrading erodes the removal (~12% of captured CO2 per 1% CH4 lost)
Transport to the nearest operating well is costly (~$92/tCO₂)
Geologic storage only moderately accessible — transport adds cost

ranked.label: Bio-oil (hydrothermal liquefaction)
pros: Handles WET biomass (manure/biosolids) directly — no drying needed
Hydrothermal liquefaction densifies the carbon into a stable bio-crude, cheap to haul to distant wells
Viable where wet-slurry injection/AD would need nearby geologic storage
Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Net of counterfactual debits: 50% gross − 9 pts soil carbon the spread manure would have built (50-yr) − 11 pts replacement fertilizer
Higher cost and earlier-stage than pyrolysis or direct injection
Lower CDR efficiency than slurry injection (~50% vs >90%)

ranked.label: AD + CCS (all biogas carbon)
pros: Manure is already digested here — AD+CCS retrofits existing biogas plants
Suits wet feedstock; mature digestion technology

cons: Only ~40% of manure carbon is captured — much of it stays in the digestate
Dilute flue-gas (or fuel-cell) capture at small plant scale is costly

Geologic storage only moderately accessible — transport adds cost

caveats: Nearest affordable storage is a pending Class VI application (Meadowbrook / Carbon Connect (Strathcona)), speculative (~30-50% reach injection, multi-year) — counted only as a fallback; storage access capped at 'moderate'.

BC: much harvest slash is piled and burned for fire-hazard abatement — it is part of the forestry residue above (not additional), and diverting it is a near-term, high-additionality supply. No primary volume or spatial data exist (one secondary estimate: ~3.9 Mt CO₂ from BC slash-pile burning in 2019, UBC policy brief, unverified). Community fuel treatments (BC CRI program) are small (~6,000 ha completed, 2013-2023).
